title: The Barista and Your Mood
text:
Research on happiness usually focuses on close relationships. In 2014 Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn of the University of British Columbia looked at the people we barely know: classmates, neighbors, the person who makes our coffee.

In one set of studies, students tracked their interactions with classmates over a term, and adults counted their daily interactions with close friends and family and with more casual acquaintances. On days when people had more interactions than usual with weak ties, they reported being happier and feeling a greater sense of belonging, even after accounting for their contact with close ties.

In a related experiment published the same year, the researchers sent people into a busy Starbucks with one of two instructions. Some were told to be efficient: have the money ready and keep the exchange with the cashier brief. Others were told to have a genuine interaction: smile, make eye contact and have a short conversation. Those who had a genuine interaction left in a better mood and with a stronger sense of connection than those who had rushed through. They spent only a few moments longer, but those moments mattered.
lesson: Brief friendly exchanges with acquaintances and strangers lift your mood and sense of belonging. Smile and say a few real words to the people you pass every day.
location: University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada
source: Sandstrom, G. M., and Dunn, E. W. (2014). Social interactions and well-being: The surprising power of weak ties. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 40(7), 910-922. Also: Sandstrom, G. M., and Dunn, E. W. (2014). Is efficiency overrated? Minimal social interactions lead to belonging and positive affect. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 5(4), 437-442.
